content.title: About
content.content: Ham or pork pieces cooked in a savory gravy are a classic dish in British and American cuisine. The meat is usually cured, smoked or boiled, then simmered in a sauce made from stock, cream and spices, resulting in a tender, flavorful product.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “ham” historically refers to the hind leg of a pig, which is often cured and smoked.
Gravy originated in medieval England as a way to use the pan drippings left after roasting meat.
In the United States the dish is commonly served with mashed potatoes, while in the United Kingdom it is often paired with Yorkshire pudding.
There is a “country ham” variety that is aged for several months, giving it a stronger flavor.
Traditional gravy may include ground black pepper, cloves, onion and sometimes a touch of sugar to balance the taste.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: The iron in pork is highly bioavailable, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fat content makes the dish a good source of energy, especially in colder months.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cured ham can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A high amount of saturated fat may affect blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens such as salmonella.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sliced thinly, alongside mashed potatoes, rice, vegetable ragout or crusty bread. For a lighter version, garnish with fresh herbs like parsley or rosemary.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked ham in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen ham can be stored for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
